transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what's been troubling you or what brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, thank you. Um, well, I guess... where do I even start? I actually ended up calling the employee assistance program at my company. I'm a sales manager, so, you know, there's always a lot of moving parts, always a lot of pressure and things on my plate, but... what finally pushed me to actually pick up the phone and call them is that I am just... I'm barely sleeping right. It's been driving me absolutely crazy. 

I'll get into bed, right? And instead of just drifting off like a normal person, I just lie there. My brain just won't shut up. I'm constantly replaying every little detail from work, every conversation, every account I'm managing, and then... then it just bleeds into replaying these arguments I've been having at home lately. Just playing the tape over and over in my head, thinking about what I said or what I should have said. And if I do finally manage to exhaust myself enough to pass out, it doesn't even matter because my eyes just snap open at, like, 3 or 4 in the morning. Almost every night. 3 AM, 4 AM, just staring at the ceiling in the dark, and the whole cycle starts over again. 

By the time my actual alarm goes off and I have to get up and get ready for the office, I have to start the whole day feeling like I never even closed my eyes. It's like I never really rested at all, just this heavy, dragging feeling. I just couldn't keep doing it on my own, so the EAP suggested I come talk to someone.
Have you noticed that you’re not enjoying things the way you used to, like activities or hobbies that you used to find pleasurable?

Yeah, actually, that’s... that’s been really bothering me, too. I used to be a pretty active guy, always having something on the calendar to look forward to, you know? Like, I used to play pickup basketball a couple of times a week, just to sweat it out and leave the office behind, and we had these regular bowling nights with some buddies. I was usually the one organizing things. I'd even plan these big trips for music festivals in the summer—coordinating the tickets, the travel, getting the whole group together. 

And on weekends, my absolute favorite thing was firing up the smoker for my friends. I have this really nice heavy-duty offset smoker, and I’d spend twelve, fourteen hours doing a brisket or ribs, making my own rubs from scratch, having everyone hang out in the backyard. It was my thing, it was how I unwound. 

But lately... I don't know. I just don't care. The guys will text me about basketball or bowling, and I just stare at the group chat trying to come up with an excuse. I end up canceling on them half the time. And even when I don't cancel—like if I feel too guilty and I actually force myself to drag my feet and show up—I'm not really *there*. I'm just standing around, totally checked out, feeling like I'm just going through the motions. I'm throwing the ball or whatever, but I'm just waiting for it to be over so I can go home. I haven't even taken the cover off my smoker in I don't know how long. It just feels like way too much effort now, and there's no payoff, no joy in it anymore. It's just strange because these were the things that used to keep me sane, and now I just... I can't even be bothered to pretend I'm having a good time.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, not just when you're thinking about work or the arguments at home?

Yeah, that’s exactly it. And that’s what’s so confusing about it to me, because you’d think, you know, if I just close my laptop or if everyone at home is getting along for the evening, I’d feel fine. But I don't. It’s not just when I’m actively stressing out about a big account or dealing with the tension in the house. 

Most days, it’s just... I don't know, it's like this heavy, gray mood just follows me everywhere I go. Like it’s physically attached to me. I’ll be sitting at my desk at the office, and maybe it’s a quiet afternoon, nobody’s bothering me, the numbers are fine, but I still just feel kind of hollow inside. And then I'll pack up my briefcase, I walk out to the parking garage, I get in my car... and you’d think the change of scenery would help, right? Like, it's the commute, time to decompress, maybe listen to a podcast. But I'll just sit there in traffic, I don't even turn the radio on half the time anymore, and that same gray cloud is just sitting right there in the passenger seat with me. 

Then I pull into the driveway, I walk through the front door into the house, and it’s still with me. It just follows me from the office to the car to the house, step by step. Even on a weekend when absolutely nothing specific is happening—no fires to put out at work, no arguments, just a completely blank schedule—I just feel... empty. Hollow. It’s just this constant, dull, heavy feeling that never really lifts, no matter where I am or what I'm doing. It's like my whole baseline has just dropped, and it takes so much energy just to carry that weight around all day.
Have you noticed yourself moving more slowly than usual, or on the flip side, feeling restless and unable to sit still?

Well, restless isn't really the word for it. Honestly, it’s the exact opposite. It’s more like... like I’m moving through molasses or something. 

You know, people at work—my boss, the other managers—they probably wouldn’t say I’m completely falling apart or anything. I mean, I’m still showing up, I'm still putting on the suit and sitting in my office. I've gotten pretty good at masking it, I guess. But internally, and just physically, I can absolutely tell that I just move slower. Everything takes more effort. Like, I’ll get to my desk in the morning, and I’ll open up my laptop to look at our sales dashboard or go through my inbox, and... I just sit there staring at it. Way longer than I should. I'll have a spreadsheet open and I'm just looking at the grid, not even processing the numbers, just sort of frozen there staring at the screen while the minutes tick by. 

And it gets really noticeable to me when my team needs me. I have a team of sales reps who report to me, and they’re always popping their heads into my office for quick approvals or advice, you know, the standard stuff. And lately, they’ll ask me something completely simple—like, "Hey, did we sign off on that discount for the Smith account?" or "Where did you put the new pricing sheets?"—and it's like my brain has to boot up from scratch. I just sit there for a second, taking a beat too long to actually answer them. There's just this weird lag time. It used to be a split-second response, boom, boom, boom, moving on to the next thing. But now it’s like I have to manually process the question, figure out how to move my mouth, and force the words out. I don't know if they've picked up on that delay yet, but I definitely notice it, and it's incredibly frustrating to just feel so... sluggish all the time.
Have you found yourself feeling guilty or worthless, or have you had any thoughts about hurting yourself or not wanting to live?

No, no, I haven't had any thoughts about hurting myself or anything like that. I don't want to die. But the guilt... man, the guilt is just constantly there, just eating away at me. 

It’s like my brain has this highlight reel of every mistake I’ve ever made, and it just plays on a loop all day. I keep replaying every late night at work, you know? All those times I swore to my wife I'd be home by six for dinner, but then I'd get caught up trying to close a deal or running numbers with the reps, and I'd walk in at eight or nine and the kids are already asleep. I used to tell myself I was doing it for the family, to provide for them, to get that next promotion, but now I just look back and feel sick about it. 

And it's not just work, it's the personal stuff, too. I think about all the weekends I spent focused entirely on myself. Like every tailgate I organized down at the stadium, spending the whole Saturday out drinking beers and grilling with the guys while my wife was stuck at home wrangling the kids by herself. I just took it for granted that I deserved that time. Or I'll just suddenly fixate on every dumb purchase I've made over the years—like dropping way too much money on that heavy-duty smoker I mentioned, or buying expensive golf clubs I barely even use, when that money should have gone to the kids' college funds or, I don't know, doing something nice for my wife. 

It just all piles up in my head, this massive mountain of evidence of what a terrible partner I've been. I just sit there analyzing it all, and I end up thinking my wife and kids got stuck with a selfish guy who keeps letting them down. They deserve so much better than me. They deserve someone who actually puts them first instead of his job or his buddies or his hobbies, and I just can't stop obsessing over how badly I've failed them. It just goes round and round in my head, and I can't turn it off.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight lately—like eating significantly less than usual or losing weight without trying?

It’s actually kind of a weird contradiction, to be honest. Because, yes, my appetite has been completely off, and I mean it’s been exactly like this for months now. I used to be the guy who’d organize a lunch outing with the sales reps, you know, head down to the deli or grab something from the food trucks downtown, but lately... I just don't even care about food. I’ll get into the office, pour myself a cup of coffee from the breakroom, and I will literally just run on that coffee straight through lunch. I don't even feel hungry. The hours just tick by, I'm staring at my screen like I mentioned before, and I don't even think about eating. 

And then I get home, and my wife always tries to have a nice dinner ready for us so we can sit down as a family—which just adds to that guilt I was talking about, by the way, because she puts in the effort—and I’ll sit there at the table and just... pick at it. I'll move the food around my plate, maybe take a bite or two of whatever she made, but I just can't bring myself to eat a full meal. It just feels like too much effort to chew and swallow, as ridiculous as that sounds. I just pick at dinner with my family while they talk about their day.

But the crazy thing is, you’d think with me basically skipping lunch and barely touching dinner, I’d be dropping pounds, right? Like you were asking, losing weight without trying. But it’s the exact opposite. I was getting dressed for work the other morning, putting on my standard suit pants, and I went to buckle my belt... and I realized it's sitting a whole notch tighter than it used to. I actually had to force it to the next hole. So I’m barely eating, my appetite is totally shot, but I'm somehow putting on weight. It’s incredibly frustrating. It’s like my body is just holding onto everything, or my metabolism just completely crashed along with my energy levels. So, yeah, I'm eating significantly less, but my clothes are actually getting tighter.
Have you felt a noticeable loss of energy or felt fatigued almost every day, even when you haven’t been doing anything physically or mentally demanding?

Honestly, no, not really. I know I just said a few minutes ago that I feel sluggish and like I'm moving through molasses, but that's... I don't think that's a lack of energy, if that makes sense. It's not like I'm physically tired or fatigued. 

It’s actually kind of strange, because with the way my brain is lagging, you’d think I’d be completely wiped out all the time, but I'm not. I still have plenty of physical energy. Like, I’m up at 5:30 AM every day without fail. I don't even really need an alarm most days, I just wake up. And I go through my whole morning routine—shower, shave, iron a shirt, get the suit on—and I drive the 45 minutes in heavy rush hour traffic down to the office, and I never feel like I need to pull over or take a nap. I'm not fighting off sleep at my desk, either. Even when I'm just sitting there staring at my spreadsheets like I told you, not doing anything mentally demanding at all, I don't feel drowsy. 

And it's the same on the weekends. Like this past Saturday, I spent a good three or four hours out in the yard. We have these massive oak trees in the back, and the leaves are just absolutely relentless this time of year, so I was out there raking, bagging everything up, dragging these heavy yard waste bags to the curb. And physically? I felt totally fine. I wasn't winded, my muscles weren't exhausted, I wasn't dragging my feet. I could probably go run a couple of miles right now if I had my gym clothes with me. So, no, I wouldn't say I've lost any energy or feel fatigued on a daily basis. My body feels like it has plenty of gas in the tank, it's just... I just don't really know what to do with it, I guess. But the physical energy itself is definitely still there.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant loss of energy or increased fatigue nearly every day, which is a key symptom for differentiating between major depressive disorder severity levels.
doctor.question: Have you felt a noticeable loss of energy or felt fatigued almost every day, even when you haven’t been doing anything physically or mentally demanding?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about fatigue or loss of energy, which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Honestly, no, not really. I know I just said a few minutes ago that I feel sluggish and like I'm moving through molasses, but that's... I don't think that's a lack of energy, if that makes sense. It's not like I'm physically tired or fatigued. 

It’s actually kind of strange, because with the way my brain is lagging, you’d think I’d be completely wiped out all the time, but I'm not. I still have plenty of physical energy. Like, I’m up at 5:30 AM every day without fail. I don't even really need an alarm most days, I just wake up. And I go through my whole morning routine—shower, shave, iron a shirt, get the suit on—and I drive the 45 minutes in heavy rush hour traffic down to the office, and I never feel like I need to pull over or take a nap. I'm not fighting off sleep at my desk, either. Even when I'm just sitting there staring at my spreadsheets like I told you, not doing anything mentally demanding at all, I don't feel drowsy. 

And it's the same on the weekends. Like this past Saturday, I spent a good three or four hours out in the yard. We have these massive oak trees in the back, and the leaves are just absolutely relentless this time of year, so I was out there raking, bagging everything up, dragging these heavy yard waste bags to the curb. And physically? I felt totally fine. I wasn't winded, my muscles weren't exhausted, I wasn't dragging my feet. I could probably go run a couple of miles right now if I had my gym clothes with me. So, no, I wouldn't say I've lost any energy or feel fatigued on a daily basis. My body feels like it has plenty of gas in the tank, it's just... I just don't really know what to do with it, I guess. But the physical energy itself is definitely still there.

inference.note: The patient ruled out a loss of energy or fatigue, which is a required criterion for F32.2 (Moderate depressive episode). This leaves F32.3 (Severe depressive episode) as the most consistent diagnosis given the severity of symptoms including persistent depressed mood, anhedonia, psychomotor retardation, guilt, insomnia, and weight changes despite reduced appetite.

opening_question.intent: Identify the patient's chief complaint or reason for seeking help
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what's been troubling you or what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a major depressive episode characterized by persistent depressed mood, loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities, sleep disturbance (middle insomnia), psychomotor retardation, feelings of guilt, and appetite disturbance with weight gain. These symptoms meet the criteria for a moderate to severe depressive episode without psychotic features. The episode has been ongoing for months, meeting duration requirements. There is no evidence of a prior manic or hypomanic episode, ruling out bipolar disorder. The symptoms are not better explained by an adjustment disorder or another psychiatric condition.
